notes.1a: Almost all candidates recorded results for five experiments and were able to record correct values for the volumes of sulfuric acid and water. The volume of gas collected in each experiment should have increased from experiment 1 to experiment 5. However, some candidates obtained results that did not follow this pattern or obtained gas volumes that were much lower than expected, this is probably a result of delays in inserting the bung or the bung not being properly inserted, both of which would result in the loss of gas.
notes.1b: Many excellent graphs were seen. Some candidates made things difficult for themselves by selecting a y -axis scale that was difficult to use. When plotting graphs, scales should be chosen such that the plotted data takes up over half of the available space. It is recommended that each major grid line should be equivalent to 1, 2, or 5 (or those numbers multiplied by 10 ). Candidates who chose difficult scales often did not gain credit for plotting the points. Some candidates struggled to draw an acceptable curve of best fit; a line which meanders from point to point is not a curve of best fit. The expected line should have been a curve of decreasing negative gradient.
notes.1c: Many candidates performed well on this question. To gain credit for the extrapolation, the extrapolation had to follow on smoothly from the graph line and not take a sudden change of direction.
notes.1di: Many well set out calculations were seen. The most common errors were incorrect rounding of an otherwise correct number or an error in the units.
notes.1dii: This was very well answered with almost all candidates selecting the experiment with the largest volume of gas collected.
notes.1ei: Almost all candidates could correctly state that a pipette was more accurate than a measuring cylinder.
notes.1eii: This proved more demanding than (i) , however, many correct answers were still seen. Non-credit worthy answers often focused on the difficulty of using a pipette or its fragility. Some candidates thought that the fact that a pipette could only measure a set volume of 25 cm was a disadvantage, but as that is the volume required it was not a problem in this instance.
notes.1f: The expected, and often seen, answer was ‘gas syringe’. A burette was not accepted as it is not graduated all the way to the tap and so the gas volume recorded would not be accurate.
notes.1g: The best responses explained the advantage of the modified apparatus. Many answers suggested that candidates had done less practical work that usual this year and were not familiar with the problem of gas escaping before the bung was reinserted.
notes.2a: Many candidates were able to report the formation of a green precipitate that dissolved in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. A significant number of candidates reported other observations, such as fizzing or the formation of white precipitate. This suggests that the candidates had not used the correct reagents for the test.
notes.2b: Some candidates were able to report the expected formation of a grey-green precipitate which did not redissolve; other candidates reported wholly impossible observations for the reagents that should have been used.
notes.2c: Correct observations for the positive chloride ion test were seen frequently.
notes.2d: This was expected to be an unfamiliar reaction for many of the candidates. Many candidates correctly reported either the formation of a precipitate or fizzing.
notes.2e: Most candidates who had made correct observations in (a) were able to correctly identify the chromium( III ) ion. Correct identification of the chloride ion was more common.
notes.2f: Many correct flame test colours were seen. It was also evident that some candidates are not aware of what a flame test is, giving answers such as ‘squeaky pop’ or ‘fizzing’, which have no connection with a flame test.
notes.2gi: Most candidates correctly reported the formation of bubbles. The question asked candidates to test the gas produced. When this is asked, it is expected that candidates will record the test and the result for the gas test that gave a positive result. Negative gas test results do not need to be recorded.
notes.2gii: Many candidates correctly identified the gas as carbon dioxide.
notes.2hi: Many candidates were able to correctly identify the potassium ion from the flame test result in (f) . It was not uncommon for candidates to suggest the cation was copper( II ), presumably due the observation made in (h)(ii) and forgetting that aqueous copper( II ) sulfate was the test reagent they had added to solution J.
notes.2hii: The majority of candidates reported the formation of a green or blue precipitate.
